extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of natural philosophy, evolutionary theory, geology, chemistry, biology, and sociology
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and explain the general principles by which unlike units or forces become separated and like units or forces become integrated across physical, chemical, geological, biological, mental, and social domains. Emphasizes causal relations between incident forces and resulting segregation/integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform force produces differential modification and segregation
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform force falling on any aggregate produces unlike modifications in its different parts—turns the uniform into the multiform and the multiform into the more multiform; this transformation consists of molecular rearrangements (chemical), larger transpositions (mechanical), or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret as a causal rubric: when evaluating an instance of separation, ask whether a uniform (or resultant) force acts differently on different parts of an aggregate. Examples: wind sorting fragments, electrical/magnetic attraction separating components. Anti-pattern: attributing segregation to vague 'intrinsic tendencies' without identifying differing effects of the same incident force on different parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of permanently effective force between molecular change and mechanical motion
rubrics_metrics.description: So much of the permanently effective force that reaches each part may be expended in modifying mutual relations of constituents (molecular/chemical) or in moving the part to another place (mechanical), or partially in both; if little is absorbed in one effect, much must show in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing processes, determine how incident force energy partitions into rearrangement versus movement. Example: in a compound unit, if little force produces chemical change, expect motion of the unit; conversely, low mechanical transposition implies molecular alteration. Use this to predict outcomes or explain why particular separations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of parts leads to similarity of motion; dissimilarity leads to differing motion and segregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts that are similar to each other will be similarly acted on by the force and will similarly react on it; parts that are dissimilar will be dissimilarly acted on and will dissimilarly react. Thus, incident force transformed into mechanical motion will produce like motions in like units and unlike motions in unlike units, leading to segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply as a test: check whether groups of like units experienced similar forces/motions and thus were transported/coalesced together. Examples: large fragments falling near source, dust carried further; soluble vs insoluble substances during percolation. Anti-pattern: expecting identical behavior among parts that differ materially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of separation proportional to definiteness of difference between units
rubrics_metrics.description: The definiteness of the separation is in proportion to the definiteness of the difference between the units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to gauge how sharply components will segregate: sharply different kinds (pebbles vs dust; soluble vs insoluble salts) segregate distinctly; finely gradated differences (sizes close together; alcohol/water mixture) produce imperfect separation. Example guidance: distillation of alcohol and water is difficult because their atoms are comparatively alike—separation occurs only in a narrow temperature range and incompletely if heated unduly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight differences require adjusted incident forces to become separable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed units which differ but slightly are moved in but slightly different ways by incident forces, and can therefore be separated only by such adjustments of the incident forces as allow slight differences to become appreciable factors in the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting separation of near-homologous components, expect need for precise, controlled conditions (e.g., careful temperature control in distillation; repeated re-crystallization). Anti-pattern: assuming coarse methods will suffice for near-homologous mixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed forces are segregated by reaction of uniform matter (inverse relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed forces are segregated by the reaction of uniform matters in the same way that mixed matters are segregated by uniform forces; e.g., dispersion of refracted light separates undulations (colors) because different orders are deflected at different angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when analyzing phenomena where 'forces' (wavelengths, frequencies, modes) are separated by interaction with a medium: spectrum formation, differential absorption (short undulations absorbed sooner). Example: refraction and absorption of light; adjacent parallel beams through unlike substances diverge. Use as an explanatory criterion in optical and wave phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units of like kind exposed to unlike forces segregate (like-by-unlike principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When like units are exposed to unlike forces (in amount or direction), the similarly conditioned part separates from the dissimilarly conditioned—i.e., like units subject to different resultant forces segregate and integrate separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to interpret large-scale structures (nebular rings, star/planet formation): local differences in resultant forces cause adjacent groups of like atoms to move in opposite directions and integrate separately. Example: Laplace's nebulous ring—equatorial portions acquire centrifugal force and separate from contracting mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aqueous/geologic sorting by momentum, friction, and gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed fragments differing in sizes or weights, when exposed to the momentum and friction of water and to Earth's attraction, are selected from each other and united into groups of comparatively like fragments; separation is definite in proportion to differences of the units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sedimentary deposits or shore sorting, use grain size, specific gravity, exposure to waves/tides to predict spatial sorting: fine sediments deposited farther, coarse sands nearer, boulders on top. Example: sheltered coves accumulate small pebbles; exposed ends have progressively larger stones. Anti-pattern: ignoring hydrodynamic sorting when interpreting sediment distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature and cooling-rate control segregation during crystallization and igneous cooling
rubrics_metrics.description: When several salts of different constitution are dissolved together, those dissimilar in constitution crystallize separately; isomorphous salts may co-crystallize. During slow cooling of molten rock, differential mobility over time allows mutual polar forces to segregate constituents into crystals; longer fluidity yields larger crystals (center vs sides of dykes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for interpreting mineral formation and crystal purity: rapid crystallization traps impurities, repeated re-solutions and crystallizations reduce contamination. In igneous contexts, slow cooling favors segregation of quartz, feldspar, mica into distinct crystals (granite), while rapid cooling yields more uniform trap/basalt. Example: isomorphous salts (e.g., nitrates/sulphates) may not separate except under special conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical pressures/tensions as agents of segregation in organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In organisms, mechanical pressures and tensions cause segregation: parts exposed to common strains integrate, while parts exposed to different forces retain separateness; repeated exposure can lead to coalescence (e.g., vertebral fusion, formation of sacrum, cannon bone formation in ungulates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to morphological/evolutionary interpretation: where bones or parts share a common functional strain, expect fusion or coalescence; where functions differ, expect retention of separate elements. Examples: sacrum formed by vertebrae exposed to common strain; metacarpals fuse or reduce when toes no longer act separately (ox, horse). Use as causal rubric in functional morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection as continual purification/segregation of species
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation and maintenance of a species as an assemblage of similar organisms is explained: uniform incident forces continually separate those individuals departing from the common type (unfit), leaving behind those fit—thus preserving species uniformity (segregation of like by expelling unlike).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing species integrity or variance, consider whether uniform environmental/selection pressures are acting to remove divergent individuals. Use as explanatory criterion for why species remain uniform in certain conditions and diverge into varieties where incident forces differ. Example: analogous to wind picking out autumn leaves from green ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental classification via segregation of like impressions through repeated experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental evolution consists in formation of groups of like objects and relations: repeated impressions superpose similar molecular modifications in nervous elements, generating internal ideas for a genus or species; likeness in incident forces causes integration (classification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when analyzing cognitive categorization: repeated similar stimuli strengthen common neural pathways producing stable ideas/classifications; differing stimuli create separate pathways/ideas. Examples: botanist recognizing species by repeated similar impressions; co-evolution of classification of relations with classification of objects. Anti-pattern: treating classification as arbitrary without reference to frequency and similarity of impressions.
